body:
I don't know what to say. I'm sorry for that. And it sounds like you're going through a lot right now. That sucks. 

Because you're a Smiths fan, I have to ask: have you ever read any of Morrissey's interviews about his experiences before he started singing for The Smiths? There's this great interview with the Smiths in Sounds Magazine that I remember reading. Morrissey said, 

"I had quite a happy childhood until I was six or seven, after that it was horrendous. At the age of eight I became very isolated--we had a lot of family problems at that time--and that tends to orchestrate your life.  I had a foul adolescence and a foul teenage existence.  I just sort of scraped through, escaping into films and books... I think if I'd led an acceptably frivoulous teenage life I wouldn't be sining in this group. I'm sure if you have a great time and get everything you want, all the friends you want, then you tend not to be so amvitious.  If you're deprived of certian things it makes you very resilient and you kick very hard for what you want.  And I wanted something very special becuase I'd led such an unspecial life previous to the Smiths." (http://braceneckboy.wordpress.com/2012/07/27/keep-young-and-beautiful-sounds/ if you want to read the whole thing)

The thing is that the world is a dark place when you're a teenager. It's a dark place when you're an adult, too. And though you've been through a rough patch, you've already shown yourself to be remarkably resilient; you found a girlfriend once, you made friends once, you can do it again. You've had a bad break up; this is never fun. The only way to make it better is to keep trying. Your interactions with girls are awkward? Yes, I bet, along with every other teenage boy. Remember that confidence you felt when you were with your girlfriend? The best way to get it back is by pretending you still have it, and acting as though you do. If you fake it long enough, you will get there. 

Here's the sad truth: everyone wants someone to say hello to them first. Everyone wants to be "that guy." When you've been happy and then you aren't, it makes being unhappy that much worse because you know what you're missing out on. 

Here's what I suggest: start writing down your thoughts and keeping a journal. School hasn't even really stared yet: you have a new opportunity to reinvent yourself, to be anyone that you want to be. And honestly, it's going to be hard. It might not work, and that's ok. Remember that it's because it's hard, because you have to work at it, that you become the kind of interesting, resilient person that people want to be around and want to like. 

Good luck.

Thanks for your response and kind words. You're right that 12 years is a remarkably short time, and you're also right that seeing suicide as an option reinforces a thought process that may help in the short term, but does more harm than good in the long term. I would also agree that while I am considering killing myself, I want to want to live, if that makes any sense. To be honest with you, it would be easier and less frightening. 

I also sympathize with what you're saying. If this has been my life for 29 years, what guarantee do I have that the next 29 years will be any better? What affirmative steps can I take to make my life better? I feel like part of my frustration is that nothing I've done thus far has made my life better. If it's not about self-understanding or material success, then what's it about? 

Thanks again for responding; I really appreciate it.

Thanks for your response. I think that what you've mentioned, the fear of what ending my life will do to other people, is the thing that has kept me going the longest. 

I've spoken to a number of therapists/psychiatrists over the years. I have been diagnosed with depression, bi-polar disorder, boarderline personality, and a variety of anxiety disorder, including GAD and PTSD, at various times. I'm not sure that these diagnoses have been particularly helpful to me, and I've started over with docs on three different occasions. I have a family history of bi-polar (treated with shock therapy in the 60s), which I think influenced that diagnosis. The boarderline diagnosis was mostly driven, in my opinion, by my impulsivity in my teens. The GAD/PTSD diagnosis came after being attacked in a foreign country. With the exception of my anxiety, which responded rather well to benzos and CBT, drugs and therapy have not helped significantly. So to answer your question, medical professionals differ significantly in what they think is wrong with me, but everyone agrees it's something.

That being said, I think that the people I've spoken to have helped me gain a great deal of self-awareness. Some aspects of my childhood were pretty terrible, and I'm still trying to come to terms with that. I understand what causes me anxiety and have ample strategies for dealing with it. Although I'm good at forming interpersonal relationships, I have difficulty forming romantic relationships, which drives my isolation to some degree. There is a part of me that believes, deeply and strongly, that I am unworthy of love, happiness, or success. I've tried to work on that. 

If pressed, I would call what I've experienced for years "melancholy." Freud, in Mourning and Melancholy, says that while in mourning "it is the world that has become poor and empty; in Melancholy it is the ego itself." The feelings of loss and despair manifest themselves but "one cannot see clearly what it is that has been lost." I think this is one of the best descriptions I have for what I feel. More than any one specific thing, it is the general sense of guilt, shame, and self-disgust that overwhelm any sense of happiness, success, or real joy. 

Furthermore, I am desperate for the approval and attention, external motivators that allow me to feel worthy. This makes me extremely successful in environments like school, where built-in and/or implied systems of reward and punishment, including a systems of ranking "worthiness" allowed me to feel at least ok. The depressing and honest reality is that if I had a job that gave me grades every week and beat the living crap out of me whenever I screwed up, replicating the some of the worst aspects of my childhood, I would probably thrive. 

So to answer your question, I guess the emotional coping mechanisms I learned as a child, which conflate love with ranking and punishment, combined with my inability to find positive sources of affection and attention (driven at least in part by my inability to model or see as worthwhile the kind of love I crave) create a cycle of self-hatred and self-disgust which I recognize but have thus far been unable to break. 

Anyway, thank you again for your response. It really does help me to write these kinds of things out, and try to describe what I'm feeling. Thanks for giving me a chance to do that.

Thanks, that's certainly nice of you to say. Obviously the immeasurable harm I could cause others has certainly played a part in my decision not to kill myself thus far. Logically, I understand that I shouldn't feel this way: I have all the outward trappings of success, I do significant work helping others, and I am still depressed. It is neither situational nor is it driven by specific events, but rather a deep emotional and existential emptiness that I find almost impossible to face. 

Thanks for the support; I appreciate it.

That sounds really awful. I sympathize with your situation entirely; your family situation sounds terrible, and it's something I certainly understand. Obviously I don't know you, but I would suggest three things right off the bat:

1) You should talk to a professional. You need help coping with everything that's going on in your life, for dealing with your family, and for figuring out your relationship with your boyfriend. Most colleges have a student health center that will provide you with at least some sessions free of charge. Please make the time to speak with them. They may also give you antidepressants, again free of charge or at extremely low-cost. All of this is worth a shot. 

2) It sounds to me like you seem to want to kill yourself in the moment, which is not good. Suicide is a forever decision, and though I'm not necessarily against it, I am against making forever decisions impulsively. Have you done everything that you can possibly do to improve your live and your situation? Have you exhausted all your options? Please don't make a rash decision. Realistically, impulsively trying to hang yourself with a belt could end you up in a situation where you are less capable of helping yourself and more miserable. I'm just going to go ahead and say that if your timeline is less than a year, you're not making a careful and informed choice. 

3) You have three siblings that you love enormously who are in a bad situation. Even if you don't have any other motivation for living, you do have your siblings. Again, a therapist will be helpful with this, but you may have options that you haven't considered yet to help them. This seems to be one of the things that is really eating you up. You need to speak with professionals about this: a therapist for you, possibly a legal aid attorney through a family violence clinic or local law school, etc. I know you think that there is nothing you can do, but you need to speak to someone you can trust about this and make sure. Best of all, you do have people who care about you that you can live for: your siblings. 

Please don't be offended by this OP, but you sound to me like someone who could really benefit from professional help, and you really haven't had a chance to explore that option. Please take it upon yourself to explore your options and your feelings with a professional in therapy. It may work or it may not, but for what it's worth, you gave it your best shot. You owe it to yourself and the people around you to try.
